title: A bound turns 'out of memory later' into a decision now
caption: The producer outruns the consumer by 150/s. A queue of 1 000 fills in about 7 s, and then the full queue has to push back.

steps.text: Work arrives at 400/s but the consumer can only finish 250/s, so the backlog grows by 150 items every second.
The consumer drains at its own fixed pace. More waiting doesn't make it faster: it only makes every item wait longer.
With max depth 1 000, the queue is full after 1 000 ÷ 150 ≈ 7 s. From then on it must signal upstream: block the producer, reject the item, or tell it to slow down.

scenarios.name: Consumer slows down
scenarios.summary: The database gets slow and the consumer drops to 100/s. The bound is hit in about 3 s instead of 7, and then you must block (delay moves upstream) or shed (work is lost).

steps.text: A dependency slows down and the consumer now finishes only 100 items/s.
Arrivals don't change, so the backlog grows by 300/s and the queue is full after about 3 s.
Block: the producer waits for space, with a timeout. Nothing is lost, and the slowdown travels upstream to whoever called it.
Shed: reject with 429 + Retry-After. The producer and its callers stay fast, and the rejected work must be retried or dropped.

scenarios.name: Risk: no bound
scenarios.summary: An unbounded queue never says no, so it turns overload into growing latency, then an out-of-memory crash that loses everything queued.

steps.text: Same overload: 400/s in, 250/s out. Nothing ever pushes back, so the producer keeps going at full speed.
After a minute the queue holds 9 000 items and the newest waits 36 s. Most of their callers have already timed out.
The consumer keeps working through items nobody is waiting for any more, while fresh requests queue behind them.
Memory runs out and the process is killed, taking every queued item with it. Mitigation: bound the queue to seconds of work and decide what happens when it's full.

scenarios.name: Alternative: consumer pulls
scenarios.summary: The producer appends to a durable log and the consumer pulls at its own pace. It can't be overrun; the backlog becomes lag on disk, bounded by retention.

steps.text: The producer appends to a log on disk. Appends are cheap, and disk holds days of work instead of seconds.
The consumer asks for the next batch only when it has finished the last one, so it never gets more than it can handle.
The gap between the newest offset and the consumer's offset is the lag. It grows by 150/s, and that's the metric to alert and autoscale on.
Trade-off: good for background work that may lag. A user waiting for an answer still needs a bound and a fast 'no' at the front.
